theme: Praise the LORD who executes justice, the Beatitudes’ God
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 146. Read it as the Beatitudes in song form: a psalm about the God who blesses the poor, the hungry, and the oppressed. Notice the warning in verses 3 and 4 and the blessing in verse 5.
settingTheScene: Psalm 146 is the first of the five closing Hallelujah psalms, and its theme matches the Sermon on the Mount you have just read. It is a praise song that centers on the character of God as the helper of the helpless. Jesus’ opening words in the Sermon, “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” sound much like this psalm’s “Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob.”
observation: “I will praise the LORD as long as I live” (v. 2).
“Put not your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation” (v. 3).
“When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish” (v. 4).
“Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God” (v. 5).
“Who executes justice for the oppressed, who gives food to the hungry” (v. 7).
“The LORD opens the eyes of the blind” (v. 8).
“The LORD will reign forever, your God, O Zion, to all generations” (v. 10).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with the writer talking to his own soul: “Praise the LORD, O my soul!” He decides to praise for as long as he lives. Then comes a warning: do not trust princes, mortals, or any human leader as your final hope. Their breath leaves them, they return to dust, and their plans die with them. This is not cynicism about human government but realism. No leader can save you.

The alternative is the God of Jacob. He made heaven and earth and the sea, and he keeps faith forever. That last line is the foundation of everything. God’s faithfulness is not temporary. And what does this God do? He executes justice for the oppressed, gives food to the hungry, sets prisoners free, opens the eyes of the blind, lifts up those who are bowed down, loves the righteous, watches over strangers, and upholds the widow and fatherless.

Now read the Gospels in this light. When Jesus heals the blind, feeds the hungry, and welcomes the outsiders in the chapters ahead, he is doing what this psalm says the LORD does. John the Baptist will ask from prison whether Jesus is the one who is to come, and Jesus will answer by pointing to the blind who see and the poor who hear good news. The psalm tells us what to look for.

The psalm ends with “the LORD will reign forever.” Princes die. The king lives. Our hope rests there.
connection: Matthew 11:2-6 shows Jesus answering John with the very works this psalm describes. Luke 4:18-19 has Jesus reading Isaiah 61 about good news to the poor, liberty to captives, and sight to the blind. Isaiah 2:22 says to stop regarding man, whose breath is in his nostrils. Jeremiah 17:5-8 contrasts trust in man with trust in the LORD. James 1:27 says pure religion is to visit orphans and widows. Revelation 11:15 declares that he shall reign forever and ever.
application:
Think about where you might be putting too much trust in a leader, a party, or a system. Re-center your hope on the LORD.

Choose one group named in verses 7 to 9 (the hungry, the oppressed, the foreigner, the widow, the orphan) and do one concrete thing to help.

Praise the LORD out loud today, with your whole soul, for something specific.
prayerPrompts: Praise God as long as you live, in your own words.
Confess where you trust in princes instead of him.
Thank him that he keeps faith forever and executes justice for the oppressed.
